title: Data Integrity: What You Read Is What You Wrote
subtitle: Prove that correct user data can be restored in time
summary: Data integrity is judged through users’ ability to access correct data, so intact but inaccessible backups are not a sufficient success condition. Recovery requirements should determine backup frequency, retention, location, and format. Replication protects against some failures but promptly copies bad deletions and corruption, making independent defenses necessary. The chapter combines soft deletion, tiered backups, and out-of-band validation to detect problems early and preserve recoverable history. At large scale, sharding and incremental work reduce copying costs, while long incremental chains complicate restores. Gmail and Google Music recovery cases show the value of rehearsed procedures and the difficulty of delayed detection, cross-store references, and offline media logistics. Continuous end-to-end restore tests provide evidence that recovery still works as systems evolve.

concepts.title: Recovery as the objective
concepts.body: A backup is useful for disaster recovery only when the application can load it and make data available within an acceptable time. Archive retention alone does not demonstrate this capability. Define how much recent data can be lost and how long users can wait, then test the whole restore path, including capacity, dependencies, format compatibility, and post-processing needed for actual user access.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: A database export passes a checksum test but is inadequate if restoring its indexes takes longer than the service can tolerate.

concepts.title: Independent layers of protection
concepts.body: Replication copies valid changes quickly, but also propagates accidental deletion and corruption. Soft deletion preserves a limited opportunity to undo mistakes; tiered backups provide older or more isolated recovery points. The layers should differ enough to survive relevant common failures. Retention and deletion delays must also fit the product’s privacy commitments, rather than accumulating copies indefinitely.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: A bad application deletion reaches every replica, while an isolated earlier backup still contains the missing records.

concepts.title: Early validation of application invariants
concepts.body: Storage consistency does not guarantee that application relationships remain correct. Independent validators can check invariants such as whether a listed file has corresponding contents, detecting slow corruption before usable recovery points disappear. Validators need monitoring, investigation logs, ownership, and rate limits so they do not overload serving systems. Product teams define meaningful invariants while shared infrastructure can provide the execution framework.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: A validator notices metadata referencing absent audio before a deletion defect spreads through another month of backups.

concepts.title: Restore engineering at scale
concepts.body: Large datasets require parallel, well-balanced shards and incremental processing to make verification and restoration timely. However, a long sequence of dependent incremental backups increases restore complexity and failure exposure. Recovery must also reconcile data and metadata from compatible points in time. Automated end-to-end exercises reveal missing media, insufficient capacity, broken tools, and schema drift before a real incident forces reliance on them.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: A restore rehearsal checks that recovered objects are reachable through the current application, not merely present on disk.

misconceptions.correction: They protect against certain infrastructure failures but may all receive the same erroneous mutation.

misconceptions.claim: A successful backup job proves that recovery works.
misconceptions.correction: Only a tested restore through to usable application data verifies the complete recovery path.

scenario.title: Prove what users received
scenario.context: A replicated profile store returns data after a regional failover. A checksum mismatch appears on one replica, but serving traffic is still possible from two healthy copies.

options.label: Quarantine the mismatched replica and validate before repair
options.benefit: Users read from verified copies and the corruption boundary stays known.
options.cost: The healthy copies carry more load during validation.
options.consequence: The team routes around the replica, verifies checksums, and rebuilds it.

options.label: Accept the replica and repair asynchronously
options.benefit: Availability remains high and repair starts immediately.
options.cost: Bad data can spread or be read before repair completes.
options.consequence: A later read exposes corrupted profile data to customers.

scenario.debrief: Isolating a suspect copy prevents unverified data from reaching users, but replica repair covers only some failure modes. Also test recovery from application corruption that reaches every replica, including restoring coherent data and metadata.

quiz.question: Which failure can ordinary synchronous replication spread?
options: Loss of the only historical snapshot after all live replicas stay correct
A site outage that leaves healthy remote replicas reachable
quiz.explanation: Replication deliberately propagates mutations, including harmful ones.

quiz.question: Why is early detection especially valuable for creeping corruption?
options: It makes historical backups unnecessary for application errors
It lets validators scan without competing for serving resources
It limits propagation and preserves more usable recovery points
quiz.explanation: Delay makes both the affected state and the reconstruction problem grow.

quiz.question: What is the strongest evidence that a backup strategy meets its purpose?
options: A full backup completing within the nightly maintenance window
An end-to-end restore delivering correct accessible data within the target time
Every replica reporting the same current database size
quiz.explanation: The required outcome is usable restored data, not a successfully written file.

exercise.title: Prove a data recovery
exercise.prompt: Choose a harmful deletion or corruption scenario and define a restore exercise that ends with correct data available through the application.

fields.label: Loss scenario
fields.placeholder: What is the cause, scope, detection delay, and last known correct state?

fields.label: Recovery point
fields.placeholder: Which independent backup or soft-deletion layer survives this failure?

fields.label: Proof
fields.placeholder: How will you verify user access, cross-store references, elapsed restore time, and recent data loss?

steps.text: Check application invariants before corruption spreads.
Prevent known bad data or further harmful mutations from propagating.
Recover from an independent suitable point in history.
Verify that users can reach correct data within the target time.
